Q1.text: TinyML systems lack a widely accepted and easily reproducible benchmark, which limits continued progress in the field.
Without a fair, reliable comparison method, direct comparison of TinyML solutions is challenging and the impact of individual optimizations is difficult to measure.

Q2.text: Edge/TinyML inference is argued to increase energy efficiency, privacy, responsiveness, and autonomy of edge devices by avoiding wireless-communication energy costs.
TinyML is argued to enable a class of smart, battery-powered, always-on applications for real-time data collection and processing.
The paper motivates the benchmark by noting that TinyML achieves ML inference under a milliwatt of power, breaking the traditional power barrier limiting distributed machine intelligence.

Q3.text: EEMBC's CoreMark benchmark does not profile full programs and does not accurately represent machine learning inference workloads.
EEMBC's MLMark benchmark uses models too large for MCU-class devices, requiring far too much memory, and does not support power measurement.
The existing large-scale MLPerf inference benchmark precludes MCUs and other resource-constrained platforms due to a lack of small benchmarks and compatible implementations.

Q4.text: The authors created MLPerf Tiny, the first industry-standard benchmark suite for ultra-low-power TinyML systems, comprising four benchmarks: keyword spotting, visual wake words, image classification, and anomaly detection.
Each of the four benchmarks specifies a dataset, a reference model, and a quality target (Table 1).
The suite defines closed and open submission divisions with different rules on what may be modified from the reference implementation.
A measurement framework computes accuracy (Top-1 or AUC), latency (median inferences-per-second of five runs), and energy (median micro-Joules/inference of five runs).

Q5.text: The modular design was chosen so submitters can demonstrate the benefit of their product regardless of where it falls on the ML deployment stack, in a fair and reproducible manner.
The closed division was designed to enable a more direct comparison of systems by requiring the same models, datasets, and quality targets as the reference implementation.
The open division was designed to let submitters demonstrate improvements to performance, energy, or accuracy at any stage of the ML pipeline.
Feature extraction was excluded from the keyword-spotting measurement window because it is typically a small fraction of overall compute cost.

Q6.text: Reference-model accuracy was evaluated for each of the four benchmarks using per-benchmark test/evaluation subsets.
Reference implementation latency and energy were measured on the NUCLEO-L4R5ZI board and reported in Figure 5, but the numeric values are not present in the extracted paper text.
A first round of submissions (June 2021), spanning closed and open divisions across five hardware/software stacks, was collected and qualitatively summarized in Table 2.

Q7.text: The KWS reference DS-CNN model achieved 92.2% accuracy in the authors' experiments; the quantized model reached 91.6% on the full test set and 91.7% on a 1000-utterance subset (target 90%).
The IC reference ResNet model achieved 86.5% accuracy on 200 CIFAR-10 test images (target 85%).
The VWW reference MobileNetV1 model reached about 86% accuracy on the preprocessed MSCOCO 2014 test dataset (target 80%).
The AD reference autoencoder achieved AUC 0.88 (fp32) and AUC 0.86 (quantized) on 248 evaluation samples (target 0.85).

Q8.text: The results establish that each reference implementation (52.5-325 KB model size) meets its own stated minimum accuracy target.

The results establish that a first round of five submissions, across closed and open divisions on diverse hardware (ARM MCU, RISC-V MCU, RasPi 4, an NN accelerator, an FPGA), successfully exercised the benchmark's modular design.
The results establish that 8-bit integer quantization was the most common numerical format among first-round submitters.

Q9.text: The paper's extracted text does not contain numeric latency or energy values; those results exist only in Figure 5, an image not recoverable from this snapshot.

The current benchmark version excludes pre-processing/feature extraction from the measurement window, so its results do not reflect full end-to-end pipeline cost (a scope boundary the authors state directly).
None of the first-round submissions modified the training dataset, so the round-one results do not demonstrate data-centric optimization.
Because the closed division prohibits any retraining or weight replacement, closed-division results cannot be read as evidence about retraining or architecture-search effects.

Q10.text: The primary contribution is MLPerf Tiny, the first industry-standard benchmark suite for ultra-low-power TinyML systems, developed collaboratively by more than 50 organizations.
The contribution includes open-source reference implementations (training scripts, pre-trained models, C code) for the four benchmarks.
The contribution includes a measurement framework and closed/open division run rules for comparing accuracy, latency, and energy.

Q11.text: The authors state the suite must continue to evolve with new benchmarks for domains like wearables, medical devices, and environmental monitoring, while also keeping a subset of benchmarks long-term stable for historical tracking.

For streaming, time-domain tasks (KWS, AD), limited bandwidth between the test runner and the device under test makes it difficult to recreate a true streaming scenario without added data-transfer delays.
Excluding feature extraction from measurement while allowing submitter-selected feature choices creates a possible degenerate case where nearly the whole model could be labeled 'feature extraction'.
The closed division's models are based mainly on FC and CNN layers; broader architectures such as RNNs are not yet covered by the reference suite.

Q12.text: MLPerf Tiny is a four-benchmark suite (KWS, VWW, IC, AD) for ultra-low-power TinyML inference, measuring accuracy, latency, and energy.
It has closed (strict: same model/dataset/quality target) and open (flexible, must still document deviations) submission divisions.
Reference accuracies were 92.2%/91.6-91.7% (KWS), 86.5% (IC), about 86% (VWW), and AUC 0.88/0.86 (AD) - each above its stated quality target.
